# Evidence Review — IMF MAC-010 (Mexico 2022 Article IV)

I verified each claim against the exact code-bound source excerpt and locator. Below are the results.

---

## ACCEPT (18)

| evidence_id | Basis |
|---|---|
| EF-Ec845a8a2d23f | "authorities expect that these subsidies will cost around 2 percent of GDP" — fuel price stabilization and food programs both present. |
| EF-E0d3203a14fd6 | "lowering inflation by an estimated 2 percentage points" at "around 1.5 percent of GDP" budgetary cost; disproportionate benefit and price-signal dilution both stated. |
| EF-E39eb4efd183e | "higher food and energy prices have only increased the deficit by around ¼ percent of GDP with fuel subsidies offset by higher oil revenues." |
| EF-E5dd35040bd89 | All four reforms listed verbatim; revenue increases of 1.0 and 0.6 percent of GDP between 2019 and 2022 stated (though these are expected/projected figures — see LIMITATION). |
| EF-E0edf3523cee1 | "CA deficit is projected to increase to around 1 percent of GDP" — the 1% figure for 2022 is directly supported. |
| EF-E0cd6fe160411 | "total capital adequacy ratio has increased to over 19 percent, from 16 percent before the pandemic." |
| EF-Ec07649629788 | "EBA model estimating a cyclically adjusted CA norm of -1.2 percent of GDP, implying a CA gap of -0.2 percent of GDP." Both figures verbatim. |
| EF-Eb8758815aa98 | "current account posted a deficit of 0.4 percent of GDP in 2021 and is expected to widen to around 1 percent." |
| EF-Ef352ea6d9f58 | April 2021 legislation; September 2021 deadline; 87% and 70% reduction in subcontracted employment; "no apparent change in total employment" — all verbatim. |
| EF-E8887941d7c47 | "56.8 percent of the rural population in poverty… compared to 57.7 percent in 2018" and "40.1 percent of urban households… up from 36.8 percent in 2018" — both verbatim. |
| EF-Ec289ed363ded | "raise the minimum wage from 42 percent of the median formal sector wage in 2018 to 59 percent in 2022" and "real per capita labor income of about 5 percent (y/y) by mid-2022" — both verbatim. Attribution qualified ("may have contributed"). |
| EF-E9603d5b8fc15 | "Headline inflation rose from about 3 percent at the end of 2020 to 7.4 percent by end-2021 and to 8.7 percent by August" and "food inflation… 14.1 percent in August." Both verbatim. |
| EF-Ece8dbfd34166 | GDP figures -8.1% (2020), 4.8% (2021), 2.1% (2022), 1.2% (2023) appear verbatim in the national accounts table. |
| EF-Ea821cad22d7e | New electricity law "replaced auctions by nonmarket-based policies, with regulatory power given to the CFE"; "created conflicts of interest and disrupted contracts signed under the 2013 reform." Both present. |
| EF-Ea4c008a112dd | GDP projections 2.1% (2022) and 1.2% (2023) appear verbatim in the table. |
| EF-E7b02797e3919 | "successive and gradually larger increases in the reference rate brought the ex ante real policy rate… to a moderately restrictive level by September 2022 at about 4 percent." Verbatim. |
| EF-Ea14f1a09b27b | "Reported earnings more than doubled to over USD 23 billion in the first six months of 2022 compared to the same period last year." |
| EF-E10133c6fe1ee | "National unemployment rate (annual average) 3.3 3.5 4.4 4.1 3.4 3.7" — 4.4 (2020) to 3.4 (2022) confirmed. "Manufacturing jobs were relatively insulated and recovered early while construction has lagged" verbatim. |

---

## REJECT (12)

| evidence_id | Rejection Reason |
|---|---|
| **EF-E613e64d72a22** | Combined figure of MEX$541,223 million (1.86% GDP) is not present anywhere in the excerpt (page 74). The excerpt shows fuel MEX$395.4 billion + food MEX$72,823 million = MEX$468,223 million (≈1.61% GDP). |
| **EF-E36583d529735** | Same combined total (MEX$541,223 million, 1.86% GDP) not verifiable from page 74 excerpt. Food program items individually sum to MEX$72,823 million (0.25% GDP) which is confirmed, but the combined fuel+food total is not. |
| **EF-E51b1e176f2e0** | ARA metric claim states **131%** but excerpt states **125%** — a 6-percentage-point discrepancy beyond rounding tolerance. USD 207.7 billion vs excerpt's USD 208 billion is minor, but the ARA discrepancy is material. |
| **EF-E92bf7816ad6e** | Claim states USD 205.7 billion for 2022; excerpt page 11 references USD 205.7 billion for 2022 but then page 57 excerpt shows USD 208 billion (2021). The 125% ARA figure appears on page 11, not the claimed 131%. USD and ARA figures cannot both be correct as stated. |
| **EF-E82e4717989ea** | "Cumulative increase of approximately 50.4 percent" is mathematically unsound: (59−42)/42 ≈ 40.5%, not 50.4%. The 50.4% figure does not appear in the excerpt. |
| **EF-E7bf2ae0e6452** | No TFP data appears in the page 26 excerpt. The excerpt contains only a note about WGI normalization and confidence intervals. The entire TFP claim (negative/flat over 1990-2020, supply-side impediments) is unsupported by this locator. |
| **EF-Eabb33c70bf12** | The 8.1% core inflation figure does not appear in the page 2 excerpt. The excerpt confirms headline 8.7% (Aug 2022) and 8.5% (end-2022 projected), but not the 8.1% core value. |
| **EF-E6140839dabd4** | The informality rate "above 55 percent in 2022" cannot be verified from the page 48 table. The table contains unemployment figures (3.4% 2022 confirmed) but does not display an informality rate value of 55% or any specific 2022 informality figure. The chart on page 32 showing 2005–2022 is the proper locator but is not cited. |
| **EF-E73af0449f713** | Same issue: the page 32 chart is the proper source, but the page 32 excerpt_end_char 192 cuts off the chart data entirely. The 55% informality figure for 2022 cannot be confirmed from this truncated excerpt. |
| **EF-Edfc272f7c654** | The quantities (56.2% 2022; 57.7% 2023) appear in the table but the claim's sequence implies 2022=56.2% and 2023=57.7%, yet the table shows 57.6% for a prior year and 57.7% for the projected year — the year mapping is ambiguous. Additionally, the excerpt does not directly state "sustainable with high probability over the extended time horizon"; this characterization appears elsewhere in the Annex III text. |
| **EF-E1d615e69e849** | Causal attribution — claim states the rate path was to "bring inflation back to the 3 percent target." The 3% target is not stated in the page 10 excerpt; the excerpt only describes the policy rate level and market terminal-rate expectations. The causal rationale is inferred, not sourced. |
| **EF-E7b02797e3919** | Same causal issue: the excerpt does not explicitly connect Banxico's rate path to returning inflation to 3%. The "3 percent target" is absent from the page 17 excerpt. |

---

## ATTRIBUTION LIMITATIONS (not rejections; advisory)

The following accepted items present IMF staff figures as though they were direct government statements or unauthenticated data. These should be flagged for reformulation but do not warrant rejection:

- **EF-Ea5614fb66252** — The proposed 2023 budget with deficit increasing to 4.1% is sourced from an IMF staff calculations table ("Source: IMF staff calculations"). Claim presents it as a Mexican government action without attribution to the IMF.
- **EF-E5d5cb1d8080a** — Revenue increases of 1.0% and 0.6% of GDP are characterized as confirmed outcomes; the source says "expected increases," indicating projected figures.
- **EF-Ea4c008a112dd** and **EF-Ece8dbfd34166** — GDP growth figures are IMF staff projections, not realized data. Should be attributed as projections.
- **EF-Eaf608c8a0297** — Structural primary balance "about neutral in 2023" is IMF staff calculation ("Source: IMF staff calculations").
- **EF-E2235e5c2d94a** — Pension reform details (contribution rates, minimum years) are presented as facts but sourced from an IMF Annex on Mexico's Pension System; the IMF staff characterizations ("reforms will increase pension eligibility, they might adversely affect labor market incentives") are omitted.
